title: Customer support lead

manager.name: Leah
manager.title: Head of Operations
manager.persona_note: Leah is working within a real budget limit. A good recruiter shows the trade-off kindly, so Leah can choose.

teaser: Leah needs someone to lead the support team at a fitness app, on a tight budget.
context: The company runs an app for booking fitness classes and has about 60 people.
The support team has 8 people. Most joined in the last year.
message: Hi, I need a lead for our customer support team. The team has grown quickly, and they need someone to guide them.
Money is tight this year, so I need to be careful with the budget. The old job ad is attached.
Do you have ten minutes to go over what we need?
ad: 5 or more years in customer support
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Leah will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to coach a new support team and cut how long customers wait for a reply.
needs.n2: Someone to answer the hardest customer emails themselves.
needs.n3: Someone to write a library of help articles.

beats.label: The budget
beats.sam: I need a lead for our support team, but money is tight. What can I get for $55,000?

choices.text: Before we get to numbers, what happens if the team keeps going without a lead?
choices.reply: Replies keep getting slower. Customers are already complaining.
choices.why: Asking about the cost of waiting shows what the hire is worth, which helps the budget conversation later.

choices.text: Should I see who's out there at $55,000 and report back?
choices.why: You might find someone, but you'd skip the real conversation about what the role needs.

choices.text: Honestly, do you think anyone experienced would lead a team for that?
choices.reply: Then what's the point of hiring you?
choices.why: It may be true, but saying it bluntly ends the conversation before it starts.

choices.text: How slow are replies now, and what does that cost you?
choices.reply: Two days. People cancel their memberships over it.
choices.why: A follow-up that puts a cost on the problem gives you something solid for the budget conversation.

choices.text: So it sounds like a fairly small problem for now, or is it starting to affect customers?
choices.why: A leading guess played the problem down and got a short answer.

choices.text: How did it get this far without someone stepping in?
choices.why: It sounds like blame, so the manager closes up just when you need them to open up.

beats.label: The trade-off

choices.text: Leads usually earn a bit more than that. Would you rather find a little more budget, or consider someone newer to leading?
choices.reply: Maybe someone newer to leading. Or I could find $10,000 more.
choices.why: Showing the trade-off kindly, as a question, lets the manager choose instead of feeling cornered.

choices.text: What do other leads earn here?
choices.why: A fair question, but it skips the real trade-off the manager needs to think about.

choices.text: Should I tell candidates the role pays $55,000?
choices.why: Agreeing sets up a search that's likely to struggle, and you'll be back here in a month.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: French
beats.sam: They must speak French. It's in the ad.

choices.text: How many customers write in French each week?
choices.reply: A few. And one of our agents already handles those.
choices.why: Checking a must-have against the real work shows French is already covered.

choices.text: Should I make French a requirement for every candidate?
choices.why: It sounds reasonable, but it shrinks the search on a need that's already met.

choices.text: So French is a deal-breaker for this role?
choices.why: A yes-or-no question pushed the manager to lock in a requirement that isn't actually needed.

beats.label: Doing both
beats.sam: They should answer emails and lead the team.

choices.text: Roughly how would you like their time split between coaching and answering emails?
choices.reply: Mostly coaching. Maybe a quarter of their time on emails.
choices.why: Asking about the split shows which half of the job matters most.

choices.text: That makes sense for a small team. Should I look for someone who has done both jobs at the same time?
choices.why: True, but you still don't know which half matters more to the manager.

choices.text: Is a lead who answers emails all day really leading?
choices.why: Lecturing a manager about what leadership means costs goodwill and teaches them nothing new.

beats.label: Hours
beats.sam: It's Monday to Friday, daytime hours.

choices.text: Regular hours are a real plus for candidates. Can I mention that early on?
choices.why: A simple yes on a helpful detail builds trust and gives you a selling point.

choices.text: Is there any evening work at all, even occasionally?
choices.why: It's fair to check, but it doesn't change the search, and it uses up time you could spend on what matters.

choices.text: Don't support teams usually need evening cover?
choices.why: Pushing on a detail that's already settled wastes goodwill you'll want for the bigger questions.

beats.label: Training
beats.sam: We'll train them on our tools.

choices.text: That's great. Does that mean I can consider people who haven't used your tools before?
choices.why: Agreeing to a helpful offer, and checking what it means for the search, opens up more candidates.

choices.text: How long is the training, usually?
choices.why: It's fine to ask, but it doesn't change who you'll look for, so it's not the most useful question right now.

choices.text: Aren't the tools the easy part, though?
choices.why: Brushing off a helpful offer makes it feel unappreciated, and you miss the chance to widen the search.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: Support is easy. It's just answering emails.

choices.text: What would make a great lead want this job?
choices.reply: They'd shape a new team and see results fast.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive gives you the pitch for the right person.

choices.text: So I should keep the description simple?
choices.why: That makes the job sound small, which puts off the strongest people.

choices.text: Do you think the team would describe it that way?
choices.why: Questioning the manager's view rarely changes it. A question about the job does.

candidates.name: Remi
candidates.job: Support team lead at a delivery app
facts: Cut reply times from 2 days to 4 hours

reason.n1: Coached a new team and cut reply times sharply. At $65,000 it's over the old budget, but Leah said there might be $10,000 more.

view.n1: Remi is worth stretching for. Slow replies cost us more.

candidates.name: Nell
candidates.job: Support team lead at a software company
facts: Focuses on the quality of every reply

reason.n1: A good coach, but focused on quality rather than speed. Leah said slow replies are making customers cancel.

view.n1: Nell would make us friendlier. We need faster.

reason.n1: French matches the old ad, but Leah confirmed it's already covered, and the job is coaching a team.

view.n1: Dominique fits the price, not the job.

candidates.name: Kit
candidates.job: Senior support agent at a well-known software company
facts: Looks after the company's most important customers
Known for solving the hardest problems personally

reason.n1: The most impressive record, but built on doing the work personally. Leah wants mostly coaching, with only a quarter of the time on emails.

view.n1: Kit would answer everything personally. I need them to coach.
